newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia gets first civilian defence minister.
newsitem.headline: Russia gets first civilian defence minister.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin on Wednesday told Defence Minister Igor Rodionov to quit the armed forces and become a civilian defence minister, a post traditionally held by the military.
A presidential order released by the Kremlin said Rodionov, an army general who turned 60 on December 1, had reached retirement age.
"General Rodionov is relieved from military service because he has reached retirement age," the decree said.
Yeltsin told Russian news agencies that the defence ministry would in future be headed by a civilian.

"The experience of democratic states shows that a civilian heading a defence ministry can successfully resolve the whole complex of problems of strengthening the defence capability of the state," RIA news agency quoted Yeltsin as saying.
Interfax news agency quoted the president as saying Rodionov would "continue to resolve the most complicated questions of reforming the armed forces and strengthening the army and the navy".
Rodionov was named defence minister in July this year after Yeltsin sacked the hawkish and unpopular Pavel Grachev.

Rodionov is respected in the armed forces and has been acting to consolidate his grip over Russia's top brass in order to push ahead with the complicated task of military reform, including the planned creation of a professional army.
The Russian media have said that Russia is set to reorganise the military, which was humiliated in 20 months of fighting in the rebel district of Chechnya.

A civilian defence minister would be responsible for broad policy decisions and a military-run general staff would have direct control of the armed forces, where morale is low and many soldiers have not been paid for months.

Pavel Felgenhauer, military specialist at Sevodnya newspaper, agreed civilians were needed in the Russian defence ministry to meet the challenges of democracy and market reforms, but he said Rodionov's removal from the army might not be the way to go.
"I do not think this is the right decision... the defence ministry needs a team of professional civilians who know how an army has to be organised under circumstances of a market economy," he said.

"But if Rodionov takes off his green army jacket he does not become such an expert... Rodionov is not an efficient modern lobbyist for a modern army but an old-style Soviet military professional. I do not think that this move will change anything. It is just changing hats."
He clashed with the Kremlin earlier this month when he apparently jumped the gun and said land forces commander General Vladimir Semyonov was being sacked for major violations.
The Kremlin has said Yeltsin had agreed to dismiss Semyonov but had not done so yet.
